t: Losing a large amount of blood from anywhere in the body
do: Press hard on the wound with a clean cloth and keep pressing.
Raise the part above the level of the heart if you can.
Do not let go to look — keep the pressure on while someone brings help.

t: Coughing up blood
do: Keep the person sitting up and calm.
Get to a health centre — this needs testing for TB.

t: Lips or nails turning blue, if this is new
do: Sit the person upright and loosen tight clothing.
Get help now — this means the body is not getting enough air.

t: Great difficulty breathing that does not improve with rest
do: Sit the person upright, leaning slightly forward.
Loosen anything tight around the chest and neck.
Get to help without delay.

t: The person cannot be woken
do: Lay the person on their side so vomit can drain out.
Check that nothing is blocking the throat.
Do not give anything by mouth. Get help now.

t: So weak that he faints when he stands up
do: Lay the person down with the legs raised.
Give sips of liquid once fully awake.
Get help.

t: A day or more without being able to pass urine
do: Give liquids if the person can drink.
Get to a health worker — the bladder or kidneys may be blocked.

t: A day or more without being able to drink any liquids
do: Try small sips of Rehydration Drink, a spoonful at a time.
If nothing stays down, get help now — fluid may be needed by another route.

t: Heavy vomiting, or severe diarrhoea for more than a day — or more than a few hours in a baby
do: Start Rehydration Drink immediately and keep offering it.
Keep breastfeeding a baby.
Get help if the drink will not stay down.

t: Black stools like tar, or vomit with blood in it
do: Give nothing but small sips of water.
Get to a health centre now — there is bleeding inside the gut.

t: Strong continuous belly pain with vomiting, in someone with no diarrhoea who cannot pass stool
do: Give nothing by mouth — no food, no water, no laxative, no enema.
Do not give pain medicine; it hides the signs.
Go to a hospital at once. This may need an operation.

t: Any strong continuous pain lasting more than 3 days
do: Note where the pain is and what makes it worse.
Have it examined by a health worker.

t: Stiff neck with arched back, with or without a stiff jaw
do: Keep the person quiet in a dark, cool place.
Do not delay — this can be meningitis or tetanus.
Go now, and say what you have seen when you arrive.

t: More than one fit in someone with fever or serious illness
do: Clear the space around the person; do not hold them down.
Put nothing in the mouth.
Once it stops, lay them on their side and go for help.

t: High fever above 39°C that cannot be brought down, or lasts more than 4 or 5 days
do: Cool the body with wet cloths and fan the skin.
Give acetaminophen and plenty of liquids.
If the fever will not come down, go for help.

t: Weight loss over an extended time
do: Have this examined — TB and other long illnesses begin this way.

t: Blood in the urine
do: Give plenty of liquids.
Have it examined — do not treat this at home.

t: Sores that keep growing and do not go away with treatment
do: Keep the sore clean and covered.
Have it looked at by a health worker.

t: A lump anywhere in the body that keeps getting bigger
do: Do not squeeze or cut it.
Have it examined.

t: In pregnancy: any bleeding, a swollen face with trouble seeing late on, a long delay after the waters break, or heavy bleeding
do: Lie down on the left side.
Send for a midwife or get to a health centre at once.
Keep a note of how much bleeding there has been.
